historical_timeline.summary: Anterolateral myocardial infarction in Denver; admitted to Fitzsimons Army Hospital.
Back on a full schedule; announced he would seek reelection.
Emergency bypass surgery for ileitis with bowel obstruction.
Died at Walter Reed Army Hospital after further heart attacks.

claims.statement: Dwight D. Eisenhower was born on October 14, 1890, in Denison, Texas, to David Jacob and Ida Elizabeth (Stover) Eisenhower.
During his war years Eisenhower smoked about four packs of cigarettes a day; he quit, essentially cold turkey, around 1949 at a doctor's suggestion.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Heavy former cigarette use is a major coronary risk factor; the quit year is given as approximate in the source.

claims.statement: On September 23, 1955, during a working vacation in Denver, Eisenhower played golf at Cherry Hills; chest pain woke him early on September 24, an electrocardiogram taken by a cardiac specialist from Fitzsimons Army Hospital confirmed a heart attack, and he was admitted to Fitzsimons that day.

The electrocardiogram recorded an anterolateral acute myocardial infarction with ST-segment elevation. During the golf game he had complained of what he took to be indigestion, and he was hospitalized more than 24 hours after his symptoms began.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The documented anchor for the synthetic anterior myocardial infarction and its late presentation.

claims.statement: Eisenhower remained at Fitzsimons Army Hospital from September 24 until his discharge on November 11, 1955.
By the beginning of 1956 Eisenhower had resumed a full schedule, and on February 29, 1956, he announced that he would seek reelection.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documents his return to full work about four months after the heart attack; the synthetic episode's return-to-work goal echoes it.

claims.statement: In June 1956 Eisenhower needed emergency abdominal surgery for bowel obstruction caused by ileitis (Crohn's disease); on June 9 the surgeons bypassed the diseased segment of terminal ileum rather than resecting it.
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the true-frame index date; recorded in the timeline only. No synthetic visit is scheduled from June to August.

source_links.locator: Folder #8: 1956 Hospitalizations, WRGH, includes data on ileitis surgery

claims.statement: In November 1957 Eisenhower had a cerebrovascular event that his Army medical records file as a vascular "accident" and that an Eisenhower Library oral-history summary calls a minor cerebral artery spasm.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Usually described as a minor stroke; its exact date and deficits were not confirmed in a fetched source and are not used.

Ann Whitman Diary Series, Present Illness of the President Nov. 57

claims.statement: Eisenhower had another heart attack in 1965, had his gallbladder removed in 1966, and had further heart attacks in 1968; he spent his last nine months at Walter Reed Army Hospital and died there on March 28, 1969, aged 78.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The cause of death is not stated in the cited sources.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Take over the care of a 65-year-old executive four months after an anterior myocardial infarction treated with a stent, and carry him through the first year on the CMID schedule: twelve months of dual antiplatelet therapy, a lipid goal reached with ezetimibe, blood pressure control, reassessment of left ventricular function, depression screening, staying tobacco free, and a safe return to full-time work after cardiac rehabilitation.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Eisenhower returns two weeks after lisinopril was increased to 10 mg and ezetimibe was added. He has had no dizziness, cough, or muscle aches. His home blood pressure has been 124 to 130 over 76 to 80. He is still working half days and walks 40 minutes most days without chest pain or breathlessness. He has not needed nitroglycerin. His echocardiogram and cardiology consultation were done this morning, and he was told he can return to full-time work; he plans to start next week.

encounters.display: Same-day sick visit for a nosebleed on dual antiplatelet therapy

documentation.chief_complaint: Nosebleed this morning that took about 25 minutes to stop
documentation.billing_note: Problem-oriented office visit, established patient, with control of anterior nasal hemorrhage (CPT 30901)

hpi.narrative: Mr. Eisenhower is a 65-year-old man about six and a half months after an anterior myocardial infarction treated with a drug-eluting stent, on aspirin 81 mg and ticagrelor 90 mg twice daily, who asked for a same-day visit. This morning, after blowing his nose, his right nostril began to bleed. He leaned forward and pinched his nose, but it took about 25 minutes to stop, and he soaked several handkerchiefs. Three days ago he had a brief bleed from the same side that stopped within five minutes. The office heating has been running high and his nose has felt dry and crusted for a week. He has had no bleeding from the gums, easy bruising, black stools, or blood in the urine, and no lightheadedness. He takes no ibuprofen or other NSAIDs and no supplements. He took his morning aspirin and ticagrelor and asks whether he should stop them.

referral.question: Anterior myocardial infarction about four months ago, treated out of state with a drug-eluting stent to the proximal left anterior descending artery. Please establish local cardiology care, reassess left ventricular function, and advise on his return to full-time work and on the duration of antiplatelet and beta-blocker therapy
referral.urgency: Routine, within two weeks; echocardiogram booked for the same morning
referral.pertinent_history: Presented more than a day after chest pain began, with continuing pain, and had primary PCI with one drug-eluting stent; no other significant stenosis. Hospital echocardiogram showed an ejection fraction of 45 percent with anterior and apical hypokinesis; it has not been repeated. He has just completed 36 sessions of phase 2 cardiac rehabilitation, with an exit test of 9 METs without angina, ischemic change, or arrhythmia. On aspirin 81 mg, ticagrelor 90 mg twice daily, atorvastatin 80 mg, metoprolol succinate 25 mg, and lisinopril, which I increased today to 10 mg for blood pressure 136/82 mmHg; ezetimibe added today for LDL cholesterol 78 mg/dL. Former heavy cigarette smoker, quit about seven years ago. He is a chief executive with long days and frequent travel, now working half days, and wants to return to full-time work
questions: Has his left ventricular function recovered, and is a defibrillator evaluation needed?
Is he fit to return to full-time work and to fly, and is any further testing needed first?
Do you agree with twelve months of aspirin and ticagrelor, then aspirin alone?
How long should the beta-blocker continue?
Do you agree with an LDL goal below 55 mg/dL with ezetimibe added?

consultant_note.history: Mr. Eisenhower is seen at the request of Dr. Okonkwo to establish cardiology care about four months after an anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction treated with a drug-eluting stent to the proximal left anterior descending artery at an out-of-state hospital. He presented late, more than a day after the pain began. He has completed cardiac rehabilitation and walks 40 minutes most days without angina, breathlessness, palpitations, or presyncope. He has not used nitroglycerin. He tolerates all his medicines, with forearm bruising only. He wants to return to full-time executive work, including air travel
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Outside angiography and PCI report, the hospital echocardiogram (ejection fraction 45 percent), the cardiac rehabilitation exit test, the intake ECG and laboratory results, and today's transthoracic echocardiogram and basic metabolic panel

assessment.display: Anterior myocardial infarction about four months ago
assessment.assessment: Left ventricular function has largely recovered: ejection fraction 52 percent with mild apical hypokinesis and no thrombus or aneurysm. A defibrillator evaluation is not indicated. The reassessment was due about 40 days after the infarction and is late, but the result does not change management

assessment.display: Single-vessel coronary artery disease after stenting
assessment.assessment: Complete revascularization of the culprit vessel, no angina, and 9 METs without ischemia at the end of rehabilitation. He is at low risk, and further stress testing before returning to work would not add information
LDL cholesterol 78 mg/dL on atorvastatin 80 mg. He is at very high risk (recent acute coronary syndrome, age over 65, hypertension, prior PCI), so an LDL goal below 55 mg/dL is appropriate
Blood pressure 128/78 mmHg today on metoprolol and lisinopril 10 mg; potassium and creatinine acceptable two weeks after the increase

recommendations: Return to full-time work now, building up over the first week, and resume air travel; walk during long flights
Continue aspirin 81 mg and ticagrelor 90 mg twice daily to twelve months after the infarction, then stop ticagrelor and continue aspirin for life. Do not interrupt either drug for minor bleeding
Continue metoprolol succinate 25 mg daily for at least the first year and reassess then; with hypertension it is reasonable to continue it long term
Continue atorvastatin 80 mg with ezetimibe 10 mg; recheck lipids in 4 to 12 weeks and aim for LDL cholesterol below 55 mg/dL
Continue lisinopril 10 mg with a basic metabolic panel every six months
No routine stress testing or repeat echocardiography unless symptoms change
Continue home exercise of at least 150 minutes a week; golf is fine
consultant_note.communication: Discussed with Dr. Okonkwo by telephone today; the patient agrees with the plan
consultant_note.follow_up: Primary care will manage monitoring on the CMID schedule and make the antiplatelet change at one year. Cardiology will see him again for angina, breathlessness, palpitations, syncope, or any question about therapy
